title: 10 mistakes that mattered (and, later, helped me)
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Responding to readers who wanted the balance corrected after a post about LinkedIn self-congratulation, Skelton lays out six of ten personal professional mistakes. Three are from his classroom years: not grasping learning, blaming pupils for not learning, and being too busy to reflect. Three are from headship: avoiding classrooms as an acting head, steering colleagues into writing their own curriculum, and setting the bar too high by parading an outstanding teacher. Each is told in the same pattern of what happened and what he learned. The thread running through them is that early repeated experiences make habits sticky for teachers and leaders alike, and that his career went well because he reflected on these errors rather than hid them.
points: Teachers who start out thinking teaching is about themselves get that view reinforced by isolation, so learning needs to be placed at the centre early in a career.
Responsibility runs from teacher to student: when learning fails, the first look should be at what the teacher did that got in the way.
Busyness is no substitute for reflection, which works best when practised both alone and with a trusted colleague.
School-written curriculum and showcase classroom visits can backfire, wasting time or discouraging colleagues when the bar looks unreachable.
quotes: I learned that it was my responsibility to create the conditions under which children and students could learn well in their different ways. When learning didn’t happen, I learned to look first at what I had done that got in the way of learning and what I needed to do to get it back on track.
We need to help teachers place learning at the centre of what they do as early as possible in their careers. The more sticky the preeminence of teaching becomes, the harder it is to shift.
It seemed obvious to me that my responsibility was to prepare and plan the work and give it to the children and students. It was their responsibility to learn it.

Collectively, we didn’t have the skills or background to write an effective curriculum. We ended up with something that was barely usable by those of us who had ‘written’ it and completely useless for new colleagues who joined us later.
I learned that writing a good curriculum is fiendishly tricky. I learned that adopting and amending an existing rigorously written and tried-and-tested curriculum is usually better.

I learned that good intentions are not sufficient. I had meant well, but I hadn’t thought things through about the way I introduced the idea or about the likely different responses to it driven by the range of repeated experiences that my colleagues brought with them.

I learned that with adults, too, each successive progression from Beginning to Developing to Mastering has to be carefully staged and seemingly achievable if we want or ask people to engage in a good struggle. I learned that if it isn’t, then a bad struggle happens with most 45 year-olds as much as it does with most 12 year-olds.
